intro: The Hebrew Bible has three parts. The third part is called the Ketuvim, the Writings. It is not one long story. It is a shelf of very different books. There are songs, wise sayings, a book that asks hard questions, a love poem, a brave queen, a man among lions, a sad poem and the story of going home.

Jewish tradition reads these books at special times of the year. Psalms are sung every day. The Song of Songs is read on Passover. Esther is read on Purim, with noise. Lamentations is read on Tisha B'Av. Ecclesiastes is read on Sukkot. In this unit, you will learn what each book says and when people read it.

By the end, you will know the names of these books in Hebrew and English. You will be able to find the two-line echo in a psalm. You will be able to tell the stories of Esther and Daniel. And you will know why the Tanakh ends with the words "let him go up."
bigQuestion: How do the songs, sayings and scrolls of the Ketuvim give people words for joy, sorrow, courage and hope?

timeline.t: David rules in Jerusalem; Jewish tradition connects many psalms with him
Solomon rules; tradition connects Proverbs, Ecclesiastes and the Song of Songs with him
Babylon burns the Temple in Jerusalem; Lamentations mourns the city
The exile in Babylon; the stories of Daniel and his friends are set here
Cyrus of Persia says the exiles may go home; the book of Ezra opens with his message
The Second Temple is finished in Jerusalem
The story of Esther is set in Shushan, in the Persian kingdom
Nehemiah rebuilds the wall of Jerusalem; Ezra reads the Torah aloud
A writer in Egypt speaks of the Law, the Prophets and "the other books," a sign the Writings were taking shape
Rome destroys the Second Temple; Tisha B'Av remembers both Temples
The Jewish Publication Society prints its English Tanakh, the translation this course reads
Jews read the Five Megillot on their holidays and sing the Psalms in prayer

test.q: Which part of the Hebrew Bible holds Psalms, Proverbs, Esther and Daniel?
test.why: All of these books are in the Ketuvim, the Writings, the third part of the Tanakh.

test.q: How many psalms are in the book of Psalms?
test.why: The book of Psalms, Tehillim, holds 150 songs and poems.

test.q: "The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want" opens which psalm?
test.why: Psalm 23 begins with these words and pictures God as a shepherd.

choices: A second line that echoes the first line's idea
A rhyme at the end of a line
test.why: Parallelism is the two-line echo found in Hebrew poetry, in Psalms, Proverbs and Job.
Mishlei is the Hebrew name of Proverbs, the book of wise sayings.

test.q: What do Job's friends say about his suffering?
choices: He must have done something wrong
test.why: Job's friends argue that bad things happen only to bad people, so Job must be guilty. Job says no.

test.q: Which book is read on Passover?
test.why: The Song of Songs is full of spring, so it is read on Passover.

test.q: Who planned to kill the Jews in the book of Esther?
test.why: Haman, the king's helper, planned to kill the Jews. Mordecai and Esther stopped him.

test.q: Why do people make noise during the Megillah reading on Purim?
choices: To call people to the synagogue
test.why: Each time Haman's name is read, people rattle groggers and stamp to drown it out.

test.q: What is unusual about the book of Esther?
choices: God's name is never written in it
It has no people in it
test.why: God's name does not appear in Esther. Jewish tradition reads God as hidden in the story.

test.q: Daniel was thrown into the lions' den because he did what?
choices: Kept praying after a law forbade it
test.why: A new law said no one could pray to anyone but the king. Daniel kept praying by his window.

test.q: What does Eikhah, the first word of Lamentations, mean?
test.why: Eikhah means "How!" The book asks how the busy city became so lonely.

test.q: On which holiday do families eat in a hut and read Ecclesiastes?
test.why: Ecclesiastes, Kohelet, is read on Sukkot, the fall harvest holiday with huts of branches.

test.q: What did Nehemiah lead the people to build?
test.why: Nehemiah led the rebuilding of Jerusalem's wall, finished in fifty-two days.

test.q: Which book comes last in the Tanakh, and how does it end?
test.why: The Tanakh ends with Chronicles and Cyrus's words "let him go up." A Christian Old Testament ends with Malachi.

write.prompt: The Ketuvim give people words for hard times and happy times. Pick one feeling: joy, sorrow, courage or hope. Find two or three passages from this unit that speak to it (for example Psalm 23:1, Proverbs 15:1, Job 1:21, Esther 4:14, Lamentations 1:1, Ecclesiastes 3:1 or Nehemiah 8:8). Explain what each passage says and how Jewish readers use it during the year.
tips: Name the book, chapter and verse for every passage you use.
Say "the text says" or "Jewish tradition reads"; do not say what people must believe.
Use the unit's words: Ketuvim, parallelism, Megillah, exile.
Tell when the passage is read or sung, like Purim, Sukkot or the Shabbat table.
Compare two passages instead of saying one is better.
